extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsels, PR practitioners, and students of public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations professionals on analyzing problems, audiences, creating news, and using psychological and social techniques to modify public opinion and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for changed conditions (national or local)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changed conditions — whether national or local in import and significance — must be taken into consideration by the public relations counsel if they concern in the slightest degree his particular public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political, legal, social, or local developments (from a national prohibition law to a local police edict) and incorporate their impact into PR strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit basic human instincts and desires
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic elements of human nature (desires, instincts, innate tendencies) are fixed but their directions may be turned by skillful handling; modern business avails itself of fundamentals like shelter, sex, and food to exert coercive force on publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which universal instinct(s) (e.g., desire for shelter, gustatory appeal, sex appeal) the campaign can legitimately and effectively appeal to and design imagery/slogans accordingly (examples: cozy home radiator ad; Gulden Mustard imagery; soap advertising).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use self-preservation instinct flexibly
rubrics_metrics.description: The instinct of self-preservation is highly flexible and can be appealed to in many ways (health, safety, strengthening slogans, insurance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame messages as protecting or strengthening the audience (e.g., 'Have you had your iron to-day?', insurance as safety measure; hygiene and safety appeals for products).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply MacDougall’s primary instincts as tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven primary instincts (flight-fear, repulsion-disgust, curiosity-wonder, pugnacity-anger, self-display-elation, self-abasement-subjection, parental-love-tenderness) are utilized to develop ideas and emotions to modify opinions and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map campaign elements to specific instincts: use fear for public health warnings; curiosity via advance 'feelers'; pugnacity by personifying antagonists; self-display by praising supporters; parental love via child-focused appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to fear (flight) appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Stress on possible dangers (plague, epidemic) is effective because it appeals to fear and offers prevention as a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using fear, present a plausible danger and a clear preventative action; avoid undue panic but make the prevention tangible and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use curiosity and wonder to pre-arouse interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity and wonder are continually employed (e.g., feelers sent out before an announcement; suspense in book promotions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create teasers, advance interest, puzzles or suspenseful hooks to prime the public before the main message is released ('What is wrong with this picture?' examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harness pugnacity via issues, contests, and personified antagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: Pugnacity (anger) can be used to stage combats, create issues, and personify antagonists, encouraging public engagement; contests/tests exploit this instinct to attract crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the campaign as a contest or battle when appropriate; stage debates, announce adversaries, use wartime language for campaigns (e.g., 'kill the germs', 'swat the fly'); be aware of ethical dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize ethical dangers when enlisting pugnacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pugnacity can be enlisted for decency and progress but can also be used to suppress and oppress; the dangers are those of any weapon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the social consequences of stirring conflict; avoid demagoguery and manipulation that subverts truth or harms vulnerable groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contests, issues, and opportunities for 'talking back' to draw crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversial, partisan, or conflictual subjects and occasions allowing public expression draw far larger crowds than non-controversial lectures; allowing 'talking back' increases attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When organizing events, include elements that permit public participation, controversy, or competition to boost engagement (debates, prize contests, resolutions of protest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ self-display to increase supporters’ commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Public praise and visible recognition (naming rooms, elaborate letterheads) cause lukewarm adherents to become forceful factors in a movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create avenues for public recognition (naming opportunities, public commendations) to cement allegiance and enlist influential supporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parental-love and tenderness appeals for charities and sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental love is continually employed (baby-kissing candidates, child images in charity drives) and is effective in eliciting sympathy and contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use child-focused imagery or stories to humanize causes, while ensuring dignity and ethical representation of vulnerable subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and mobilize group leaders (gregariousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Group leaders who command respect can bring their followers to a cause; selecting a cross-section of leaders helps mirror the community and amplify the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create advisory/celebration committees composed of stereotypical community leaders (banker, preacher, society woman) to lend credibility and transfer their followings to the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment publics and analyze subdivisions carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: After analyzing the problem, subdivide publics by interest, geography, age, language, education, etc.; success depends on selective capacity and approachability of leaders for each subdivision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map target audiences into specific groups, identify relevant leaders for each, and tailor appeals to the particular motivations and access channels of each subgroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage individualism alongside gregariousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to individual expression complement group appeals; self-display and individualism operate together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to group-leader strategies, create opportunities for individual recognition and personal expression to engage supporters on both communal and personal levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and manage stereotypes and mental habits (stereotypes/clichés)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes and mental habits (reflex images, clichés) are shortcuts that enable wider acceptance; the PR counsel may use, combat, or create stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify existing stereotypes to reinforce or replace (e.g., use Danube-waltz imagery to reshape Austria’s image), create new memorable slogans/phrases, and avoid overuse that renders a stereotype shop-worn ('Hundred per cent American' example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visible objects and emblems as effective symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Visible objects (national flag, instruments for scientists, white factory buildings) act as physical metaphors to symbolize abstract qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include recognizable physical symbols in events and imagery to anchor abstract claims (cleanliness, patriotism, expertise), remembering that emblems and trademarks are powerful stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit play and entertainment tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Play tendency is utilized via street fairs, fireworks, contests, and other recreational events to gather people and raise funds or goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, organize playful public events to attract broad participation and create positive associations with the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze client problem and visualize multiple public perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: First analyze the client’s problem and objective; then analyze the public by visualizing oneself as member of many publics (manufacturer, retailer, worker, financier, politician) and their subdivisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform role-based empathy exercises to surface the range of affected interests and craft appeals that resonate across those vantage points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devise a plan, choose methods and organs of distribution, and estimate interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: After analysis, devise an action plan, select distribution media, and estimate how the client’s case will strike the targeted public mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match message form and channel to audience, and anticipate feedback loops between client, message, and public reception to adjust tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the issue easy to pick out (overcome attention flicker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it easy for the public to pick the issue out of the mass of material; overcome the tendency of public attention to 'flicker' and 'relax' by simplifying and dramatizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong, compact lead elements (headlines, visuals) and isolate the single most compelling point to prevent audience attention from wandering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify and dramatize abstract or heavy facts for public consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract discussions and heavy facts must be simplified and dramatized; refinements of reason and shadings of emotion cannot reach a considerable public without simplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform technical details into clear, vivid narratives, analogies, or events that illustrate the central point; avoid overwhelming the audience with nuance in primary public messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create news — lift startling facts and isolate ideas into events
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal powerful enough to secure acceptance can be termed news; the PR counsel must create news by lifting startling facts and developing ideas into events so they claim attention in competitive news markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify surprising or consequential angles, package them as discrete events or announcements, and time releases to maximize newsworthiness and media pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use headlines and visual metaphors as compact simplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline is a compact, vivid simplification; cartoons and visual metaphors provide physical signs for vague human qualities; PR analyses should perform the same distillation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft concise, vivid headlines and imagery that encapsulate the campaign’s essence; use visual metaphors to make abstract qualities memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply truthful, accurate, and verifiable news to the press
rubrics_metrics.description: To the newspaper the PR counsel serves as a purveyor of news; conscientious counsel supplies truthful, accurate, verifiable information and is therefore valued by journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain factual accuracy and verifiability in all press materials; build relationships with journalists by consistently providing usable, honest news items (ethical obligation reinforced by editors’ codes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that 'news' is relative to the medium and paper
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes news varies by newspaper and medium; timeliness is often important but not sufficient — newspapers differ in what they consider newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor pitches to the editorial needs and audience of each medium or outlet; emphasize timeliness when appropriate but also the human-interest, novelty, or consequence angles that the target outlet prefers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallize obscure public tendencies and create resonant symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: A chief contribution of the PR counsel is to analyze obscure tendencies of the public mind and crystallize them into symbols, stereotypes, and language the public will accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use insight into nascent public moods to invent symbols or phrases that pre-exist broad public acceptance, speak the audience’s language, and frame issues before they reach full expression.
